games.explanation: The market keeps pricing the Mets like a coin flip in this series, but the Pirates are the clearly worse roster and Manaea is the better arm on the mound tonight. He's punched out nearly 29% of the hitters he's faced this year, which matters against a Pittsburgh lineup where Lowe and Reynolds are both running strikeout rates north of 26. Lindor gets the platoon look he wants against a righty, and Bichette has hit lefties and righties with equal indifference all season. Getting plus money on the stronger team, the stronger starter, and the stronger lineup is the kind of stack the board rarely hands out. +132 is the price, and it's the whole reason we're here.

Luzardo is a monster against lefties and merely mortal against righties, and Toronto happens to run out one of the most right-handed lineups in the league behind Guerrero and Springer. That platoon gap is enormous (a .215 xwOBA versus lefties balloons past .300 against righties), which is the entire reason the Jays are live as a road dog here. Bieber isn't the same guy he was, but a hot ballpark with the wind blowing out cuts both ways, and the Blue Jays are the better team by a comfortable Elo margin regardless of who's on the mound. At +180 on a coin flip that the board has priced closer to 40 percent, you take the plus wood and let the platoon splits do the work.

The White Sox as a plus-money home dog against Cleveland is the kind of line that only exists because of the logos on the jerseys. Chicago is actually the higher-rated team here by a meaningful margin, and the market hasn't caught up to the idea that this version of the Guardians offense, outside of Ramirez, doesn't scare anyone. Davis Martin is nothing special, but he doesn't have to be against a lineup where Kwan slaps singles and the rest of the order runs a barrel rate that would embarrass a Triple-A club. Getting +106 on the better team is the entire argument, and the argument is a good one.

Misiorowski misses bats and issues walks at roughly the same rate, which is a fun profile until you meet a lineup patient enough to make him prove it twice per inning. Minnesota's top righty bats, Bell and Keaschall in particular, do their damage against right-handed arms and don't chase, so the walk problem becomes a lineup problem in a hurry. The sim spits out a 4.3 to 4.3 game, which is a coin flip dressed up as a road dog, and the board is charging you for a Milwaukee blowout that the underlying math doesn't see. At +240 you only need this to be a real game, and the walks alone should get you there.

The market keeps pricing the Diamondbacks like they're the road underdog against Kershaw circa 2014, and instead they're facing a rookie left-hander whose numbers against righties are held up entirely by weak contact luck. Wrobleski gives up hard contact to right-handed bats at a genuinely alarming rate, and Arizona happens to run Carroll, Marte, and Moreno at him in a dome where the ball travels fine. Eduardo Rodriguez is nobody's ace, but the projected score sits at a near dead heat, which is not what a +131 dog is supposed to look like. Give me the better team getting plus money in a game the board has quietly turned into a coin flip.

Getting a plus number on the better team is the kind of thing you're supposed to jump on before the market catches up, and tonight the market is giving it away. Emerson Hancock is a command-lite righty who walks over a batter an inning against lefties, which is a real problem when Aranda and Díaz are waiting for him with a combined .400ish xwOBA on that side of the plate. Seymour, meanwhile, has quietly been the better arm in this game by a healthy margin, missing bats at a rate Hancock can only dream about. The roof stays shut, the park suppresses runs, and Tampa's lineup gets the pitcher it wants; +106 on the stronger side is the entire argument.
